The low cycle fatigue loops for each test condition are presented in Figure 25, providing a visual representation of the significant impact of heat treatment and surface finish on fatigue life. As anticipated, the specimens that did not undergo any heat treatment exhibited the shortest life cycle, highlighting the detrimental effects of residual stresses and internal porosity on fatigue performance. In contrast, the life cycle increased substantially as more material was removed from the surface, such as through electro-polishing and machining. Notably, the machined HIPed specimen demonstrated the best fatigue life, attributed to the removal of the most material and the elimination of all internal porosity. This specimen was fabricated by printing a cylinder and subsequently machining it to the specified geometry, with the gauge length maintained at the required size, without any reduction. UNCLASSIFIED AMMT – 316H SS Los Alamos National Laboratory Page 3-27 Establishing Peregrine Peregrine, an innovative in-situ code developed by ORNL, holds great promise for determining defects based on layer-by-layer images. In FY23, LANL secured IT approval to download and initiate developmental work on Peregrine, paving the way for its implementation in the AMMT project. Building on this momentum, FY24 saw continued efforts to assess Peregrine's capabilities on the EOS M290 and EOS M400 LPBF AM platforms. However, the FY24 development process was marked by a series of delays, primarily attributed to procurement issues and outdated software on the AM machines. Despite these challenges, the team persevered, laying the groundwork for future progress in integrating Peregrine into the AMMT project. Equipment Procurements The EOS M290 platform, in its native form, comes equipped with a 4 MP camera featuring an 8mm focal length lens. However, this built-in system fell short in providing the necessary resolution and zoom to effectively capture phenomena on the build platform, necessitating a series of strategic procurements. As FY2024 commenced, a suite of advanced sensors was ordered, including a 20 MP visible wavelength sensor, a 4 MP Near-Infrared sensor, and a 24 MP FLIR sensor, along with their accompanying accessories for seamless connectivity. These cutting-edge sensors were designed to capture high-fidelity images of the powder bed in-situ. Additionally, a new desktop computer was procured to support the upgraded sensor array, as the existing system lacked the capability to concurrently read data from the new sensors and was insufficient for training machine learning algorithms within a reasonable timeframe.
